nameStory: This tiny moss gets its 'blunt-leaved' name from the rounded, obtuse tips of its leaves - quite different from the sharp, pointed leaves of many other mosses. The 'bristle moss' part refers to the hair-like structures called peristome teeth that help disperse spores from the capsules, creating a bristly appearance around the opening.
description: Blunt-leaved Bristle Moss is a small cushion-forming moss that grows directly on tree bark and occasionally on rocks. It forms tiny, dense tufts that are easy to overlook, rarely growing more than a centimeter tall. The individual plants create small, rounded patches that look like miniature green or brownish-green cushions pressed against the bark. This epiphytic moss (a plant that grows on other plants) is quite rare in New England, making it a special find for moss enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves have distinctly blunt, rounded tips rather than sharp points, and feel slightly rough to the touch due to tiny bumps called papillae - use a hand lens to see 1-2 papillae per cell

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, tight cushions or tufts directly on tree bark, creating dense patches that feel springy when gently pressed

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found growing on the bark of trees, occasionally on stone surfaces, never on soil

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Ranges from bright green when wet to brownish-green or olive when dry, with the color change quite noticeable after rain

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: When present, the small capsules have bristle-like teeth around the opening that are visible with magnification

habitat: This epiphytic moss grows on the bark of various tree species throughout New England's forests, from lowland woods to mountain slopes. It seems to prefer mature trees with rough bark texture and can occasionally be found on rock surfaces in shaded, humid locations. Look for it in mixed hardwood-conifer forests where humidity levels remain relatively stable.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as spring moisture returns, and sporophytes may begin developing on mature plants.
seasonality.summer: Maintains steady growth during humid periods but may appear brownish during dry spells, quickly greening after rain.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most visible as deciduous canopy opens up, allowing more light while maintaining moisture from fall rains.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but less active, appearing more brownish-olive and compressed against the bark during cold, dry periods.

funFact: This moss is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only five times by citizen scientists, making each discovery feel like finding botanical treasure - you're more likely to spot a rare orchid than this tiny bark-dweller!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other small bark-growing mosses, but the combination of blunt leaf tips and the papillae (tiny bumps) on the leaves sets it apart. Memory trick: 'Blunt and bumpy' - the leaves are both blunt-tipped and have a slightly rough, bumpy texture when viewed closely.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly classified in the genus Orthotrichum and may still appear under that name in older field guides as Orthotrichum obtusifolium. The genus name Nyholmiella honors Finnish bryologist Heikki Nyholm, reflecting the important contributions Scandinavian botanists have made to moss taxonomy.
compareHints: Since this is the only Nyholmiella species in our dataset for New England, compare it with other small epiphytic mosses in the Orthotrichaceae family. Unlike many of its relatives, Blunt-leaved Bristle Moss has leaf margins that don't curl backward (non-revolute) and the distinctive 1-2 papillae per leaf cell. Most other bark mosses in this family have either pointed leaves or smooth leaf surfaces without the characteristic bumpy texture.
